summary: Defines IS-IS extensions for flooding traffic engineering information about links between autonomous systems, supporting MPLS and GMPLS inter-AS traffic engineering. The information can then be used to compute paths across AS boundaries. It does not define flooding of information from one AS into another.

eli5.summary: Roads between different countries need to be described on the map so trip planners can pick good routes. This adds those border-crossing roads to the routers' shared map.

questions: how to advertise inter-as links in is-is
is-is extensions for mpls te across autonomous systems
what is the inter-as reachability information tlv
how does is-is advertise inter-as te links
subtitle: How IS-IS advertises traffic engineering details of links between autonomous systems, now including IPv6-only routers.

tldr.problem: To compute an MPLS or GMPLS traffic engineering path across several autonomous systems, a router or PCE needs to know the TE properties of the links that connect the ASes, but IS-IS only describes links inside its own network.
tldr.mechanism: The ASBR advertises each inter-AS TE link in a new Inter-AS Reachability Information TLV (type 141), with sub-TLVs for the remote AS number and ASBR identifiers, and it proxies for the far end of the link.
tldr.outcome: This obsoletes RFC 5316 and adds support for IPv6-only operation. It floods information about inter-AS links only; it does not flood TE information from one AS into another.

today: RFC 9346 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5316, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 5305 extends IS-IS to carry traffic engineering (TE) information for links inside an area. RFC 4216 asks that a method be able to compute a path spanning multiple autonomous systems (ASes). To do this, a path computation entity (the head-end router, an AS Border Router or a Path Computation Element) needs TE information about the links that connect to other ASes.

This document defines the Inter-AS Reachability Information TLV to advertise that information, four sub-TLVs for it, and two sub-TLVs for the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV that carry the TE Router ID. The existing TE sub-TLVs from RFC 5305 and RFC 6119 can be reused inside the new TLV.

The non-objectives are explicit: no TE information is distributed from within one AS to another, no TE reachability for destinations outside the AS, no change to the PCE architecture, no TE aggregation, no exchange of private information between ASes, and no IS-IS adjacencies on the inter-AS link.
sections.eli5: Routers already know the roads inside their own country. This RFC teaches them about the border crossings too, but not what is inside the neighbouring country.

sections.title: Why Path Computation Needs Inter-AS Links
sections.content:
Two methods for inter-AS paths are discussed. In the per-domain method (RFC 5152), the path is determined one domain at a time. A router at the entry of an AS must pick an exit ASBR that connects to the next AS. In the RFC's example of three ASes and twelve routers, router R5 has three possible exit points from AS2 (R6, R7 and R8) and needs to know which of them reach AS3 and whether the bandwidth is adequate.

In the backward-recursive method (RFC 5441), Path Computation Elements cooperate along a chain of domains. Each PCE must know which ASBRs in the neighbouring AS are reached by which inter-AS link, and the link's TE properties.

Both cases need the same four items: the list of inter-AS TE links of the local AS, the TE properties of each, the AS number of the neighbouring AS, and the TE Router ID of the neighbouring ASBR. GMPLS networks may need further information. If path computation is distributed, the information is needed throughout the local AS.
sections.eli5: A trip planner at the border needs to know which crossings lead to the next country, and how wide each one is, before it picks one.

sections.title: Choosing the TE Router ID
sections.content:
A TE Router ID MUST be an address that is unique within the IS-IS domain and stable, meaning it can always be referenced in a path regardless of the state of the node's interfaces.

For IPv4, if the Traffic Engineering router ID TLV is advertised, the address SHOULD be identical to it; otherwise it MAY equal an IP interface address that meets the requirements. For IPv6, if the IPv6 TE Router ID TLV is advertised, the address SHOULD be identical to it; otherwise it MAY equal a non-link-local IPv6 interface address.

The standard TE Router ID TLVs only have area flooding scope. When the TE Router ID is needed to reach all routers in the whole IS-IS domain, it MUST have the same flooding scope as the Inter-AS Reachability Information TLV, so two sub-TLVs are defined for the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV: IPv4 TE Router ID (type 11, 4 octets) and IPv6 TE Router ID (type 12, 16 octets). An ASBR that supports TE for IPv4 and has an IPv4 TE Router ID MUST include the IPv4 sub-TLV, otherwise the IPv6 one. The IPv6 case mirrors this, and both MAY be present.
sections.eli5: Each router needs a name tag that is unique and never changes, so everyone can point to it from far away.

sections.title: The Inter-AS Reachability Information TLV
sections.content:
This TLV has type 141. Its fixed part is a 4-octet Router ID, a 3-octet Default Metric, a 1-octet Flags field and a 1-octet Sub-TLVs Length, followed by sub-TLVs of 0 to 246 octets. Compared to the extended IS reachability TLV, it replaces the 7-octet system ID and pseudonode number with the 4-octet Router ID and adds the Flags field.

Flags holds an S bit, a D bit and 6 reserved bits that MUST be zero when originated and ignored when received. If S is 1, the TLV MUST be flooded across the entire routing domain. If it is 0, the TLV MUST NOT be leaked between levels. S SHOULD be 0 to limit flooding to the IGP area of the ASBR, and MAY be 1 to reach all routers in the domain. This is an AS-wide policy choice, and implementations SHOULD provide configuration control. The D bit MUST be set when the TLV is leaked from Level 2 to Level 1, and TLVs with D set MUST NOT be leaked from Level 1 to Level 2, to prevent looping.

If the originating node does not support IPv4, the Router ID is the reserved value 0.0.0.0 and the IPv6 Local ASBR Identifier sub-TLV MUST be present. TLVs with Router ID 0.0.0.0 and no such sub-TLV MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: It is a form with a few fixed boxes and a flexible part. Two tick boxes say how far the form may be passed around.

sections.title: The Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Four sub-TLVs are defined for the new TLV. The Remote AS Number (type 24, 4 octets) names the neighbouring AS and MUST be included when advertising an inter-AS TE link. If only 2 octets are used for the AS number, the high-order 2 octets MUST be zero.

The IPv4 Remote ASBR Identifier (type 25, 4 octets) and IPv6 Remote ASBR Identifier (type 26, 16 octets) identify the remote ASBR. The one matching an address the neighbour has MUST be included, and if the neighbour lacks that address family, the other MUST be included instead. Both MAY be present. The IPv6 Local ASBR Identifier (type 45, 16 octets) is the IPv6 identifier of the advertising side.

Existing TE sub-TLVs from RFC 5305, RFC 6119 and other documents may also be included to describe the link's TE properties.
sections.eli5: The extra notes on the form say which country is next door and which border post you will reach.

sections.title: Advertising Inter-AS TE Links
sections.content:
When TE is enabled on an inter-AS link and the link is up, the ASBR SHOULD advertise it using the normal procedures of RFC 5305. When the link goes down or TE is disabled, the ASBR SHOULD withdraw the advertisement. When TE parameters change, such as available bandwidth, it SHOULD re-advertise but MUST take precautions against excessive re-advertisements. Hellos MUST NOT be exchanged over the inter-AS link, so no IS-IS adjacency is formed.

Normally both ends of a TE link emit LSPs, which lets path computation check that both directions meet the constraints. Across an AS boundary there is no peering, so the ASBR advertises information about both directions itself: it generates an additional LSP that acts as a proxy for the ASBR at the other edge. The information comes from the ASBR's knowledge of the link, its current status and usage, and configuration of the Remote AS Number and remote ASBR TE Router ID. The RFC says the source is outside its scope, and some details might come from BGP, which is an implementation matter.

Legacy routers do not know the new TLV and sub-TLVs, so they ignore them while continuing to flood the LSP. Routers or PCEs SHOULD NOT use these links to compute a path that exits an AS and immediately re-enters it through another TE link, except under specific policy configuration.
sections.eli5: The border guard on our side writes down what the other side's gate looks like too, because nobody from the other country will tell our map.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions are described as relatively minor and can be secured within the AS by existing IS-IS mechanisms such as cleartext passwords or Hashed Message Authentication Codes. Since no information is exchanged between ASes and no adjacency forms on the inter-AS link, no IS-IS security between ASes is needed.

Some of the data, such as the Remote AS Number and the Remote ASBR Identifier, is obtained manually from a neighbouring administration as part of a commercial relationship, and should be carefully checked. Wrong data could lead to an inter-AS TE LSP that traverses an unintended AS. If a BGP session exists between the ASBRs, a mismatch with the AS number in a BGP OPEN means local policy SHOULD decide whether to alert the operator or suppress the advertisement. If BGP is used to supply TE information, the inter-AS BGP session SHOULD be secured, for example as in RFC 5925.
sections.eli5: If someone gives you the wrong name for the country next door, your trips could end up in the wrong place, so check the details.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 5316
sections.content:
The substantive change is IPv6-only support. RFC 5316 allowed only a 32-bit Router ID in the TLV 141 header, which is a problem where no IPv4 address is available. This document says the Router ID should match the Traffic Engineering router ID TLV (134) if available, otherwise an IP interface address advertised by the originating IS. If the node does not support IPv4, the Router ID is 0.0.0.0 and the IPv6 Local ASBR Identifier sub-TLV must be present.

IANA registered TLV 141 (flags: not in IIH, SNP or purge, present in LSP), sub-TLVs 24, 25, 26 and 45 for it, and sub-TLVs 11 and 12 for the Router CAPABILITY TLV (top-level TLV 242).
sections.eli5: The old form only had room for one kind of address. The new one works even if a router only speaks the newer kind.

items.title: No cross-AS flooding
items.text: TE information inside one AS is not sent to another AS.

items.title: No outside reachability
items.text: No TE reachability for destinations outside the AS.

items.title: No aggregation
items.text: TE aggregation is not supported or recommended.

items.title: No adjacency
items.text: No IS-IS adjacency is formed on the inter-AS link.
